notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Proverbs 10, drawn from the sources I could reach. I note URLs for each point.

---

**v. 1: "A wise son brings joy to his father, but a foolish son grief to his mother."**

- Proverbs 10 begins a new section of the book. Chapters 1–9 form an introduction; here the collection of Solomon's two-line, single-verse wisdom sayings starts and runs through Proverbs 22:16. The sayings are largely self-contained and contrast two ways of living. (Enduring Word) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/
- "Wisdom" encompasses all moral excellence; "folly" is vice and perversity. The mother is introduced for poetic parallelism — father and mother each stand for both parents. (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- Matthew Henry notes that the comfort of parents depends greatly on their children's behaviour. This is a motive for parents to give good education and for children to live well. A foolish son adds guilt because he grieves those he ought to bring joy to — especially the mother who bore him with sorrow. (Matthew Henry) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/proverbs-10.html
- Solomon himself was the ultimate "wise son" (1 Kings 3) and brought joy to David, yet ironically also became a foolish son later (1 Kings 11). (Enduring Word) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/

**v. 2: "Ill-gotten treasures profit nothing, but righteousness brings deliverance from death."**

- "Treasures of wickedness" are wealth acquired by wrongdoing. They profit nothing "in the day of calamity." Jesus taught the same: "What shall a man be profited if he shall gain the whole world and forfeit his soul?" (Matthew 16:26). (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- "Righteousness" here includes liberality and benevolence (almsgiving), not merely justice. It delivers from death because it shows the heart is right toward God and calls down special grace. (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- David Guzik (Enduring Word) connects it to the Parable of the Rich Fool (Luke 12:16–21): that man gathered great wealth but was not rich toward God. Righteousness — being right with God — brings a benefit money cannot buy. (Enduring Word) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/
- Matthew Henry adds that God blasts ill-gotten wealth: when profit and loss are balanced, the gain cannot countervail the loss sustained by wickedness. Righteousness delivers — not necessarily from the stroke of death, but from its sting and terror. (Matthew Henry) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/proverbs-10.html

**v. 3: "The LORD does not let the righteous go hungry, but He denies the craving of the wicked."**

- The "soul" (life) of the righteous will not famish. The psalmist says, "I have been young and now am old, yet have I not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread" (Psalm 37:25). Christ taught the same principle: "Seek ye first the kingdom of God … and all these things shall be added unto you." (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- The Hebrew word translated "substance" (havvah) is better rendered "desire." God frustrates the eager longing of the wicked; they are never satisfied and get no real enjoyment from what they crave. (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- Guzik notes the principle is directed to the soul: the soul can flourish even when the body is afflicted. The wicked, being in opposition to God, have their desires frustrated; the righteous inherit eternal life and have their desire fulfilled. (Enduring Word) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/

**v. 4: "Idle hands make one poor, but diligent hands bring wealth."**

- The "slack hand" (Hebrew *caph*, the open, ineffective palm) is contrasted with the "diligent hand" (Hebrew *yad*, the hand tense and braced for vigorous work). (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- Charles Bridges noted: "Industry was the law of paradise (Genesis 2:15), and although it now bears the stamp of the Fall (Genesis 3:19), it is still a blessing and under God's providence brings wealth." (Enduring Word, citing Bridges) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/
- Matthew Henry extends the principle to spiritual matters: "Slothfulness and hypocrisy lead to spiritual poverty, but those who are fervent in spirit, serving the Lord, are likely to be rich in faith and rich in good works." (Matthew Henry) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/proverbs-10.html
- The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary notes God has ordered that man should labour for his food (Genesis 3:19; 2 Thessalonians 3:10). The lazy and slack-handed become poor and bring shame. (Garner-Howes) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/proverbs-10.html

**v. 5: "He who gathers in summer is a wise son, but he who sleeps during harvest is a disgraceful son."**

- This continues the theme of diligence from v. 4. The ant was presented earlier as an example of working in summer (Proverbs 6:6–8). "Sleeps" is literally "snores" (Vulgate: *qui stertit*). (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- John Trapp: "A well chosen season is the greatest advantage of any action, which, as it is seldom found in haste, so it is too often lost in delay." (Enduring Word, citing Trapp) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/
- Adam Clarke: "All the work of the field should be done in the season suitable to it. If summer and harvest be neglected, in vain does a man expect the fruits of autumn." (Enduring Word, citing Clarke) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/
- Bridges applies it to youth: "It is as much the will of God that the young should gather knowledge as that the farmer should gather his harvest." (Enduring Word, citing Bridges) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/

**v. 6: "Blessings are on the head of the righteous, but the mouth of the wicked conceals violence."**

- This was especially true under the Mosaic covenant where God promised to bless obedience and curse disobedience (Deuteronomy 27–28). (Enduring Word) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/
- The Pulpit Commentary takes "the mouth of the wicked concealeth violence" as the best reading: the wicked hide their violent intentions behind words, waiting for an opportunity. The contrast is between the manifest blessedness of the righteous and the secret sinister schemes of the wicked. (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- Matthew Henry: "Blessings shall be on their head as a coronet to adorn and dignify them and as a helmet to protect and secure them." The wicked's mouth is "covered with violence" — their violent dealings return on their own heads. (Matthew Henry) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/proverbs-10.html

**v. 7: "The memory of the righteous is a blessing, but the name of the wicked will rot."**

- The lasting, fragrant perfume of a holy life is contrasted with the noisomeness and quick decay of an evil name. The Pulpit Commentary asks: "Who ever thinks of calling a child Judas or Nero?" (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- Guzik: "If the wicked are remembered at all, it will be as a stinking, rotten thing." The heroes of faith in Hebrews 11 are examples of the righteous whose memory is blessed. (Enduring Word) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/
- Adam Clarke: "The very name of the wicked is as offensive as putrid carrion." (Enduring Word, citing Clarke) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/
- Matthew Henry notes this is part of the duty of survivors: "Let the memory of the just be blessed" — we should delight in making honourable mention of good people who are gone, and be followers of them in what is good. (Matthew Henry) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/proverbs-10.html

**v. 8: "A wise heart will receive commandments, but foolish lips will come to ruin."**

- The wise in heart is not proud: he accepts the divine law with all its directions and is not above learning from others. The contrast is literally "the solid in heart" versus "the loose in lips." (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- John Trapp: The wise "submit to God's holy word without replies and cavils. This is check to the brave gallants of our age, which exercise their ripe heads and fresh wits in wrestling with the truth of God." (Enduring Word, citing Trapp) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/
- Matthew Henry: The obedient "take it as a privilege … to be under government, which saves them the labour of deliberating and choosing for themselves." The disobedient are "prating fools, fools of lips, full of talk, but full of nonsense." (Matthew Henry) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/proverbs-10.html
- Garner-Howes: The wise obey and submit to proper authority, as did Abraham (Genesis 22) and the widow of Zarephath (1 Kings 17). The talkative know-it-all comes to ruin. (Garner-Howes) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/proverbs-10.html

**v. 9: "He who walks in integrity walks securely, but he who perverts his ways will be found out."**

- The one who walks in integrity has nothing to conceal or fear. He walks "securely" (Aquila: "without anxiety") because he has no secret sin. The one who deals in crooked practices "shall be known" — exposed, punished, and put to open shame. (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- Guzik: The person with no double life has no anxiety from fear of having sin discovered. He tells a story (sometimes attributed to Conan Doyle) of a man who sent letters reading "All is discovered; flee at once" — and a guilty businessman fled immediately. (Enduring Word) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/
- Matthew Henry: "He that walks uprightly … is safe under a divine protection and easy in a holy security … He knows what ground he stands on, what guide he follows, what guard he is surrounded with, and what glory he is going to." (Matthew Henry) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/proverbs-10.html
- Garner-Howes: Like the one who follows the Good Shepherd, he has nothing to fear (Psalm 23:4). But the perverse cannot hide forever; they will be found out (1 Timothy 5:25; Matthew 10:26). (Garner-Howes) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/proverbs-10.html

**v. 10: "He who winks the eye causes grief, and foolish lips will come to ruin."**

- Winking the eye is a sign of craft, malice, and complicity with wicked comrades (as in Proverbs 6:13). Ecclesiasticus 27:22: "He that winketh with the eyes worketh evil." The crafty plotter causes trouble by his cunning and secrecy. (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- The second half repeats v. 8b. The two together teach that the garrulous fool is even more certain to bring ruin than the crafty plotter. (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- Matthew Henry distinguishes: the "politic, designing, self-disguising" sinner (the winker) causes sorrow to others and himself. The "public, silly, self-exposing" sinner (the prating fool) is less dangerous — "The dog that bites is not always the dog that barks." (Matthew Henry) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/proverbs-10.html
- The LXX reads the second half differently: "a frank rebuke will make for peace." (Garner-Howes, noting the LXX) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/proverbs-10.html

**v. 11: "The mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life, but the mouth of the wicked conceals violence."**

- The righteous person's words are a "well of life" — a constant spring of wisdom, comfort, and edification. God himself is called "the well of life" (Psalm 36:9) and "the Fountain of living waters" (Jeremiah 2:13). The holy person, drawing from this supply, sheds life around. (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- Bruce Waltke: "Flowing well water is particularly precious … people gather around it. The open, benevolent speech of the righteous is just as necessary for a community, offering everyone abundant life — temporal, intellectual, moral, and spiritual." (Enduring Word, citing Waltke) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/
- The wicked, by contrast, conceal violence — they disguise harmful intentions with professions of friendship, as Joab and Judas did with a kiss. (Matthew Henry) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/proverbs-10.html

**v. 12: "Hatred stirs up dissension, but love covers all transgressions."**

- This verse is cited in 1 Peter 4:8. Hatred keeps alive old feelings of revenge; love puts aside, forgets, and forgives all offences against itself. The primary reference is to the blood feud, for which cities of refuge were established. (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- Love covers sins in two senses: it covers the sins of others (by forgiving and not exposing them) and covers the sins of the one who loves (by receiving God's forgiveness). There is a place for confrontation and exposure of sin — Proverbs 28:13 and 27:5–6 balance this. (Enduring Word, citing Kidner) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/
- Adam Clarke: "Love conciliates; removes aggravations; puts the best construction on every thing; and pours water, not oil, upon the flame." (Enduring Word, citing Clarke) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/
- Garner-Howes contrasts the tendency of hatred to provoke strife (Genesis 21:9–11; 27:41–42) with the conciliating influence of love (Genesis 45:5–8; 1 Corinthians 13:7; James 5:20). (Garner-Howes) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/proverbs-10.html

**v. 13: "Wisdom is found on the lips of the discerning, but a rod is for the back of him who lacks judgment."**

- When a person has wisdom, it will be found on their lips — what they speak reveals the wisdom they possess (cf. Matthew 12:34). (Enduring Word) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/
- The one lacking judgment (Hebrew: "wanting in heart") brings punishment on himself by his foolish talk. Adam Clarke: "He that can learn, and will not learn, should be made to learn. The rod is a most powerful instrument of knowledge. Judiciously applied, there is a lesson of profound wisdom in every twig." (Enduring Word, citing Clarke) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/
- Matthew Henry: "Those that foolishly and wilfully go on in wicked ways are preparing rods for themselves, the marks of which will be their perpetual disgrace." (Matthew Henry) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/proverbs-10.html

**v. 14: "The wise store up knowledge, but the mouth of the fool invites destruction."**

- Wise people treasure up useful knowledge for proper occasions — through memorisation, note-taking, and study. The fool, by contrast, rejects knowledge and is always uttering carelessly what brings trouble. His mouth is "near destruction." (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- Matthew Henry: "Whatever knowledge may be at any time useful to us we must lay it up, because we know not but some time or other we may have occasion for it. We must continue laying up as long as we live." (Matthew Henry) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/proverbs-10.html

**v. 15: "The wealth of the rich man is his fortified city, but poverty is the ruin of the poor."**

- This is a plain observation about how the world works: wealth gives protection and options; poverty exposes the poor to all kinds of evil, moral and material. The Hebrew word used for "poor" (*dal*) implies weakness and inability to help oneself. (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- G. Campbell Morgan: "This is a plain recognition of the power of wealth, and the paralysis of poverty. It is a wholesome corrective to much nonsense talked today about the blessings of poverty. Wealth may become a curse, but poverty is inherently a destruction." (Enduring Word, citing Morgan) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/
- Derek Kidner: "You may be called to forgo wealth; you must certainly rate it below honesty. But don't affect to despise it; don't embrace poverty out of laziness or romanticism." (Enduring Word, citing Kidner) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/
- Matthew Henry cautions that both rich and poor make common mistakes: the rich think their wealth makes them safe (it does not), and the poor think poverty ruins them (a person may live comfortably with little if content and keeping a good conscience). (Matthew Henry) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/proverbs-10.html
- Garner-Howes notes that Job said trusting riches as one's hope was iniquity (Job 31:24), and Paul urged Timothy to charge the rich to trust the living God, not uncertain riches (1 Timothy 6:17). (Garner-Howes) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/proverbs-10.html

**v. 16: "The labor of the righteous leads to life, but the gain of the wicked brings punishment."**

- Honest labour brings its own reward in God's blessing and a long and peaceful life. All the profit the wicked make they use in the service of sin, which tends to death (cf. Romans 6:21, 23). (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- Guzik: For the righteous, labour is life-giving — it is a gift to co-labour with God (1 Corinthians 3:9). The wicked have a "reward" also, and it is sin and the judgment due to it. (Enduring Word) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/
- Garner-Howes: Character, not poverty or wealth, governs the quality of one's life. The righteous use their assets to promote spiritual life; the wicked use their increase to indulge more in sin. (Garner-Howes) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/proverbs-10.html

**v. 17: "Whoever heeds instruction is on the path to life, but he who ignores reproof goes astray."**

- Wisdom and instruction must not only be gained but also kept. Keeping instruction puts one on the path of life. To refuse correction is to reject instruction and go astray. (Enduring Word) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/
- Matthew Henry: "The traveller that has missed his way, and cannot bear to be told of it and shown the right way, must needs err still, err endlessly; he certainly misses the way of life." (Matthew Henry) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/proverbs-10.html
- The Pulpit Commentary adds that instruction (Greek *paideia*) guardeth the ways of life; he who is unaffected by instruction goes astray (cf. Hebrews 12:7). (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm

**v. 18: "The one who conceals hatred has lying lips, and whoever spreads slander is a fool."**

- The verse identifies two evils: (1) The one who cherishes hatred in the heart must be a liar and hypocrite, speaking contrary to his real sentiments. (2) If he divulges his slander, he is a stupid fool, injuring his neighbour and bringing ill will on himself. (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- Adam Clarke: "How many, when full of resentment, and deadly hatred, meditating revenge and cruelty, and sometimes even murder, have pretended that they thought nothing of the injury they had sustained! Thus lying lips covered the malevolence of a wicked heart." (Enduring Word, citing Clarke) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/
- Matthew Henry: "He is especially a fool who thinks to hide anything from God; and malice is no better." (Matthew Henry) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/proverbs-10.html

**v. 19: "When words are many, sin is unavoidable, but he who restrains his lips is wise."**

- Loquacity leads to exaggeration, untruthfulness, slander, and uncharitableness (cf. Ecclesiastes 5:1–3; Matthew 12:36; James 1:26; James 3:2). (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- St. Augustine, in his *Retractations*, said of this verse: "This sentence of Scripture I greatly fear, because my numerous treatises, I know well, contain many things, if not false, at any rate idle and unnecessary." (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- Guzik: "For many people, the more they talk the more they will sin. There is much more potential sin in talking than in listening." (Enduring Word) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/

**v. 20: "The tongue of the righteous is choice silver, but the heart of the wicked has little worth."**

- "Choice silver" is tested, purified by fire. The words of the righteous are of great value. The heart of the wicked is "little worth" — mere dross by comparison. The tongue is contrasted with the heart, out of whose abundance it speaks. (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- Guzik: "For many people, the greatest riches they treasure in their hearts are the kind and encouraging things others have said to them." (Enduring Word) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/
- Garner-Howes: One's words are an index to his own worth. "The words of the just are of great value, as choice silver. The words of the wicked are of little worth, as a filing or scraping of worthless metal." (Garner-Howes) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/proverbs-10.html

**v. 21: "The lips of the righteous feed many, but fools die for lack of judgment."**

- The righteous by wise counsel teach, support, and guide others — as shepherds feed their flocks (cf. John 21:15; Acts 20:28). Fools, far from feeding others, bring ruin on themselves. (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- Garner-Howes: Through the true witness of the gospel many find eternal life (Acts 4:1–4); through the teaching of truth many are strengthened. The fool who likes his folly dies for lack of wisdom (cf. Luke 12:16–21). (Garner-Howes) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/proverbs-10.html
- Matthew Henry notes "fools die for want of a heart" — for want of thought. (Matthew Henry) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/proverbs-10.html

**v. 22: "The blessing of the LORD enriches, and He adds no sorrow to it."**

- The traditional reading: Not chance or luck, not even industry alone, but God gives the increase. When He blesses with riches, He adds no sorrow — unlike the care, fear, and grief that attend ill-gotten wealth. (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- An alternative rendering noted by the Pulpit Commentary: "And a man's own labour addeth nothing thereto" — human work must not be regarded as an equal cause of prosperity with God's favour (cf. Psalm 127:1–2). (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- Charles Bridges compared v. 4 and v. 22: "The one notes the primary source of wealth; the other points to the instrumental source of wealth. Neither can be effective without the other. The sluggard looks for prosperity without diligence; the atheist looks for prosperity only from being diligent." (Enduring Word, citing Bridges) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/
- John Trapp: "Those three vultures shall be driven away that constantly feed on the wealthy worldling's heart — care in getting, fear in keeping, grief in losing the things of this life. God giveth to his, wealth without woe, store without sore, gold without guilt." (Enduring Word, citing Trapp) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/
- Matthew Henry: "That wealth which is truly desirable, has no vexation of spirit in the enjoyment; no grief for the loss; no guilt by the abuse of it. What comes from the love of God, has the grace of God for its companion." (Matthew Henry) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/proverbs-10.html

**On the prosperity gospel debate (v. 22):** This verse is frequently cited by prosperity-gospel teachers as proof that God wants all believers materially wealthy. Sources consulted push back:

- Ligonier (Reformed): David Murray argues that in the OT, spiritual blessings were manifested in material form because the church was in its infancy. In the NT era, "Wisdom's rewards are more spiritual and eternal than material and temporary." God still blesses materially, but the focus of Christ and the Apostles is on spiritual and eternal blessings. — https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/does-proverbs-teach-health-wealth-and-prosperity-gospel
- The Gospel Coalition (Reformed/evangelical): Kevin DeYoung writes that Proverbs holds multiple truths in tension: money is a blessing from God, but it is also a great temptation; wealth is more desirable than poverty, but not as good as righteousness and the fear of the Lord. — https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/blogs/kevin-deyoung/money-and-possessions-in-proverbs/
- Bible.org (evangelical): The prosperity gospel's hermeneutics are "highly subjective and arbitrary. Bible verses are quoted in abundance without attention to grammatical indicators, semantic nuances, or literary and historical context." The Abrahamic covenant blessings are primarily spiritual (Galatians 3:14), not material entitlements. — https://bible.org/article/bankruptcy-prosperity-gospel-exercise-biblical-and-theological-ethics
- The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary explicitly states: "This is not a blanket promise that all shall be made rich, neither does it imply that labor is not necessary … God blesses with riches according to His wisdom and purpose." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/proverbs-10.html

**v. 23: "The fool delights in shameful conduct, but a man of understanding has wisdom."**

- The fool regards evil as entertainment, as sport — literally "like a laugh," child's play. There is a competitive aspect to evil among fools, each trying to outdo the other. (Enduring Word) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/
- The Pulpit Commentary notes the Revised Version better captures the sense: "And so is wisdom to a man of understanding" — the wise man finds his refreshment in living wisely, which is as pleasant to him as mischief is to the vicious. (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- Bruce Waltke: "As strong people delight in performing feats of strength and musicians find joy in their virtuosity, the competent person finds delight in constructive work." (Enduring Word, citing Waltke) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/

**v. 24: "What the wicked man dreads will overtake him, but the desire of the righteous will be granted."**

- The wicked, though he carries on his evil lightly, is troubled with the thought of retribution. That which he fears shall come upon him (cf. Job 3:25; Isaiah 66:4). (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- The righteous desire only what agrees with God's will, and this God grants — if not in this world, certainly in the life to come (cf. Psalm 37:4). (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- Garner-Howes: The wicked shrink from what they dread, but judgment is inescapable (Job 15:20–21). The desire of the righteous to see God is certain and will be the beginning of eternal glory (1 John 3:2). (Garner-Howes) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/proverbs-10.html

**v. 25: "When the whirlwind passes, the wicked are no more, but the righteous are secure forever."**

- The better translation (per LXX): "When the whirlwind is passing" — i.e., when the storm of judgment falls, the wicked are swept away, while the house built on rock remains (cf. Matthew 7:24–27). The righteous has an "everlasting foundation." (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- Adam Clarke: "As tornadoes that sweep every thing away before them; so shall the wrath of God sweep away the wicked; it shall leave him neither branch nor root." (Enduring Word, citing Clarke) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/
- Guzik: The wicked have no foundation to stand on when trouble comes. The righteous, like the wise builder on the rock, has an everlasting foundation. (Enduring Word) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/

**v. 26: "Like vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, so is the slacker to those who send him."**

- The idea is of constant and extreme irritation and disappointed expectation. Sour wine sets the teeth on edge; smoke makes the eyes smart. The lazy messenger provokes the same reaction in his employer. (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- Bruce Waltke: "The drinker expected sweet wine but instead received sour vinegar. A person preparing food expected a constructive fire … but received smoke and tears instead." (Enduring Word, citing Waltke) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-10/
- The LXX renders the last clause differently: "So is iniquity to those who practise it" — it brings only pain and vexation. (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm

**v. 27: "The fear of the LORD prolongs life, but the years of the wicked will be cut short."**

- The promise of long life as the reward of a religious life appears often in Proverbs (3:2; 9:11; 14:27). The years of the wicked shall be shortened (Psalm 55:23; Ecclesiastes 7:17). (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- Garner-Howes: This is a general principle of God's providence, not an absolute guarantee for every individual. (Garner-Howes) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/proverbs-10.html

**v. 28: "The hope of the righteous is joy, but the expectations of the wicked will perish."**

- The patient expectation of the righteous is joyful because it has a good hope of being — and is — fulfilled (cf. Romans 12:12: "Rejoicing in hope"). What the wicked eagerly hope for shall come to nothing (Proverbs 11:7; Job 8:13; Psalm 112:10). (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm

**v. 29: "The way of the LORD is a refuge to the upright, but destruction awaits those who do evil."**

- "The way of the LORD" is the way He has commanded men to walk — the way of His commandments (Psalm 25:12; 119:27). To the upright it is a fortress (as in v. 15). Doing his simple duty, a good man is safe (cf. 1 Peter 3:13). But that same way is destruction to those who neglect or disobey it. (Pulpit Commentary) — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/10.htm
- Garner-Howes notes the RSV renders it "The LORD is a stronghold" rather than "The way of the LORD." (Garner-Howes) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/proverbs-10.html

**v. 30: "The righteous will never be shaken, but the wicked will not inhabit the land."**

- This repeats the divine principle regarding occupancy of the earth: the righteous shall dwell securely; the wicked shall not (Psalm 37:9, 11, 22; Matthew 5:5). Ultimately this points to the new heavens and new earth (Revelation 21:1–4, 8). (Garner-Howes) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/proverbs-10.html

**v. 31: "The mouth of the righteous brings forth wisdom, but a perverse tongue will be cut out."**

- The righteous bring forth wisdom in their speech — "buds of wisdom that expand." The flow of perversity from wicked tongues shall be stopped — "cut out" like a diseased member. (Garner-Howes) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/proverbs-10.html

**v. 32: "The lips of the righteous know what is fitting, but the mouth of the wicked is perverse."**

- The righteous know and speak what is acceptable, timely, and gracious. The wicked speak what is perverse and distorted (cf. Matthew 12:35–37; James 3:6–8). (Garner-Howes) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/proverbs-10.html

### Summary of tradition-specific notes

**Prosperity Gospel / Word of Faith (v. 22):** As noted above, this verse is a favourite proof-text for teachers such as Kenneth Copeland and Oral Roberts, who teach that material wealth is a covenant right for believers. All the traditional sources consulted reject this reading. They affirm God does bless materially, but the verse is a general proverb, not a blanket guarantee, and NT revelation shifts the emphasis toward spiritual and eternal blessings. (See URLs under v. 22.)

**Modern scholarship (NET Bible, bibleodyssey.org):** These were not reachable within my search and fetch limits. I note that the Pulpit Commentary (19th-century Anglican) does engage with the LXX and Vulgate textual variants throughout, offering a window into older critical scholarship.
